Where would you take an out-of-town friend to visit in your district?: 
FLANELL: I’d start by taking my friend on a scenic drive through Garden of the Gods, one of Colorado’s most iconic landmarks known for its towering red rock formations, stunning mountain views, and unforgettable scenery. After taking in the natural beauty of the park, I’d head to Glen Eyrie Castle for afternoon tea. Built in the late 1800s by Colorado Springs founder William Jackson Palmer, the historic English Tudor-style castle offers a peaceful and elegant experience nestled among the foothills and rock formations of Colorado Springs.
VANDERHULE: Part of House District 14 goes right down the access points of Garden of the Gods and the Glen Eyrie Castle. Both are great places to visit for out-of-town guests.
What do residents in your district say are the community’s biggest issues, and how will you work to address them? 
FLANELL: Constituents in House District 14 consistently point to affordability as the most pressing issue facing their families. Rising housing costs, increasing energy prices, and the growing burden of regulations and fees on businesses are all contributing factors, and those costs are often passed on to consumers. To address these challenges, I support reforming Colorado’s construction defect laws to include a right-to-remedy process that encourages the development of more attainable housing while still protecting homeowners. We need policies that make it easier to build entry-level homes and expand housing opportunities for working families. On energy, I oppose mandates that drive up utility costs faster than our infrastructure can reliably support. I also believe we should avoid shutting down reliable energy sources prematurely and ensure decisions are based on cost, reliability, and capacity. Expanding consumer choice will allow homeowners to select the most practical and affordable energy options for their needs. For small businesses, we need a serious review of state mandates and operating costs, including the long-term impact of the FAMLI program, as well as excessive licensing requirements, regulatory burdens, and fees. Reducing these pressures will help businesses grow, create jobs, and keep costs lower for consumers.
VANDERHULE: Colorado has a runaway cost-of-living problem. We rank as one of the worst states for violent crime and overall crime. We strangle businesses and prosperity through radical social ideologies and business regulations. These are major issues for all Coloradans. For House District 14 specifically, housing and public schools are significant issues as well. There is not enough housing available and housing costs are too high. This means there are not enough young families moving into our communities. Our public schools are experiencing declining enrollment. More students are opting for charter schools and homeschools. The first solution to these problems is allowing more houses to be built. We need to reduce the burdensome regulations on housing and home building. The second solution is to fix Colorado public schools. We need school choice, but we also need successful public schools. Put the focus back on learning. Allow school discipline that would remove disruptive students. Reward good teachers. Remove poorly performing teachers. We need to make public schools a viable option.
This was the second year in a row the Legislature had to make deep program cuts to balance the state budget. Where can the state reduce its spending, and what is your view on how Colorado can return to a positive budget situation? 

FLANELL: The state is facing a significant budget challenge after relying on one-time federal COVID funds to support ongoing programs that should have been time-limited or structured with clear sunset provisions. At the same time, Medicaid enrollment and costs have grown faster than projected, making it essential to strengthen oversight and ensure taxpayer dollars are being used efficiently and appropriately. To address this, we need a more robust audit and accountability process that regularly evaluates program performance using clear, measurable outcomes. When programs are found to be ineffective, duplicative, or wasteful, the state should have the discipline to reform or eliminate them rather than continue automatic funding. This includes reviewing existing programs that expanded during the COVID era and determining which should be scaled back or discontinued. We should also strengthen eligibility verification and safeguards across public assistance programs to ensure benefits are directed to individuals who are legally eligible, while protecting resources for those who truly need them. Combined with targeted audits to identify fraud, waste, and abuse, this approach would improve accountability and help stabilize the budget without compromising core services.
VANDERHULE: First, Colorado has enough revenue to meet its budgetary needs. But the problem is the one-party rule of radical Democrats who are spending on social experiments and social priorities. Our Colorado Democrats are not limiting funding for state-funded abortions, trans surgeries, and illegal aliens. But this radical Legislature is willing to cut vital funding for services that go to Colorado citizens and communities. Second, fraud, waste, and abuse need to be excised from the Colorado budget. Huge amounts of funding go to nonprofits and service providers in Colorado. There needs to be active auditing and transparency about where this funding goes. Third, Colorado actively strangles local businesses. Colorado is one of the most heavily regulated states in the U.S. If you have a business, Colorado imposes radical social policies on your operations and Colorado will take more and more of your profits every year. For Colorado to return to a positive budget, we need to stop unlimited funding for radical social ideologies, we need to protect Colorado cities and families, and we need to allow Colorado businesses to thrive. When Colorado was a red state, we had all of those things: safety, security, and prosperity.
What policies should the state enact regarding the proliferation of data centers? 
FLANELL: I’d like to continue learning more about data centers and their long-term impacts before taking a firm position, but I do believe there should be reasonable safeguards in place as these facilities expand. First, local communities should have a strong voice in zoning and siting decisions to ensure nearby residents and infrastructure are not negatively impacted. Second, the financial burden of large-scale development should not be shifted onto taxpayers through increased utility or infrastructure costs. I also believe Colorado must be mindful of natural resource use, especially water and energy consumption. Wherever possible, data centers should prioritize alternative cooling methods or the use of reclaimed water instead of potable water. Facilities should also have contingency plans in place to address periods of water scarcity and increased energy demand.
VANDERHULE: I support American innovation and technological leadership, but not on the backs of Colorado families and taxpayers. Data centers are welcome if they follow the rules, respect local communities, cover their true costs, and strengthen our energy independence and way of life. I would think about policies in this order: Local control first: zoning, land use, and permitting decisions belong to cities, counties, and homeowners, not state or federal mandates. We need to defend property rights and oppose top-down imposition on rural or suburban neighborhoods. No taxpayer subsidies or corporate welfare: Data centers should not receive special tax breaks, grants, or ratepayer-funded infrastructure upgrades. They must pay for their electricity, water, roads, and grid upgrades. Energy abundance over rationing: I would argue that America needs more power. This includes nuclear, natural gas, and coal. Taxpayers should not have to subsidize the massive consumption of data centers. Data centers should not drive up residential electricity bills or strain water resources in arid states like Colorado. 
What is your view on working across the aisle, and within your own party, to advance policy? 
FLANELL: Working across the aisle is essential, especially in a Legislature where Republicans hold just 35 of 100 seats. In that environment, meaningful progress requires finding common ground on policies that genuinely improve the lives of Coloradans and have a realistic path to becoming law. I believe lasting solutions require communication and collaboration, both across party lines and within my own party. I’m willing to work with any legislator who is serious about lowering costs, strengthening communities, protecting constitutional rights, and improving the quality of life for Colorado families. I won’t support policies that expand government overreach or undermine individual freedoms. I evaluate legislation based on its real-world impact on affordability, public safety, economic opportunity, and the rights of Colorado citizens, not simply on partisan labels.
VANDERHULE: Returning political power to the people of Colorado is the main role of a Colorado legislator. Insisting on the rights and freedom of the people of Colorado is the main role of a Colorado legislator. Legislators represent the people. Therefore, the only goal of legislation should be to ensure that the people of Colorado are keeping their rights, their freedoms, their businesses, and their right to self defense. Working across the aisle is great, but only if we are finding ways to allow businesses to prosper, communities to flourish, and people to be safe. Most of the legislation over the last decade of radical one-party rule has strangled our businesses, impoverished our cities, endangered our citizens, stolen our TABOR, and emburdened us with massive debt. Coloradans do not want more legislators who are going to compromise away more of their freedoms, rights, and money. Compromise and concession can only be reached if we are finding the ways Coloradans can prosper and flourish.
What is one bill, vote or other legislative action you’ve taken that you feel best demonstrates your qualification for reelection?
FLANELL: This year, I spent much of my time in a defensive posture, working to stop or improve legislation that would have negatively impacted Colorado families and businesses. In just four months, the legislature considered more than 600 bills, reflecting both the volume and complexity of policymaking in our state. At the end of the session, it was brought to my attention that I was among the top legislators that defeated the most bills. In a state that ranks among the most regulated in the country, I consider that a meaningful accomplishment, especially given that committees like Judiciary have, at times, advanced some of the most concerning legislation in recent years. This required significant behind-the-scenes work, strategic coordination, and long hours that most people never saw. In the end, I believe it was beneficial for my constituents and for Colorado.
Are there any votes the incumbent has taken in the Legislature you disagree with? What are they and why would you have voted differently?
VANDERHULE: There are specific votes the incumbent has cast that I would disagree with. But the larger issue is that, fundamentally, the House District 14 incumbent has a differing standpoint on governing and policymaking. There is a current group of Republican legislators who believe their role is to compromise with the radical Democrats and their radical policies. These Republicans will tell you they have to compromise away your freedoms and rights because they are the minority party in the Legislature. These Republicans will tell you they have to compromise away your freedoms and rights because that will hopefully attract some of Colorado’s unaffiliated voters. There is a group of Republican legislators who enjoy being courted by lobbyists and having their favor curried by special interests. These are the same Republicans who will tell you they have no choice but to compromise away your rights and freedoms. I believe the role of a Colorado representative is to ensure the rights and freedoms of every Coloradan. There cannot be compromise with proposals, bills, or legislators who want to weaken Colorado citizens.

text:
A view of the Colorado Capitol on Jan. 25, 2024. (Quentin Young/Colorado Newsline)Coloradans will vote in primary elections June 30 to determine which candidates will represent their party in the general election in November.

The elections cover Colorado’s four statewide constitutional offices, one U.S. Senate seat, all eight of the state’s congressional districts, state legislative districts and other races. Colorado Newsline sent questionnaires to candidates in contested primary races and is publishing responses as part of its voter guide to help Coloradans make informed choices.
Ballots were scheduled to be mailed to all registered voters in Colorado starting June 8.
Voters can contact their county clerk if they have not received their ballot or check the online BallotTrax system. They can also visit the secretary of state’s website to make a plan to vote in person ahead of or on Election Day. Ballots need to be received by the county clerk by 7 p.m. on that day, so voters should mail their ballot at least eight days ahead of time or drop it off in person.
Use the Colorado General Assembly’s Find My Legislator tool to determine what House and Senate districts you live in.
Candidates often refer to the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights as TABOR. That is a constitutional amendment that limits state spending according to population and inflation growth. Everything over that cap must be returned to taxpayers via a variety of refund mechanisms outlined in state statute. TABOR also requires voter approval for new taxes.

Where would you take an out-of-town friend to visit in your district? 
SANDOVAL: As a person who has grown up in Denver my entire life, this is a question I get a lot. People often ask me where to go and how to really experience Denver, and I take a lot of pride in being kind of an unofficial ambassador for my city. Depending on the season, I’d probably take them to a Rockies game at Coors Field. They may not win, but there’s not a bad seat in the stadium. You get a 360 view of the game, an amazing look at the downtown skyline, and views of the mountains usually paired with one of those world-famous Colorado sunsets. I’d also take them down to the Santa Fe Arts District. We could grab a coffee at Tonantzin Casa de Café or get a bite to eat somewhere along Santa Fe while walking around La Alma–Lincoln Park, one of Denver’s oldest neighborhoods and the city’s first historic cultural district honoring the Chicano Movement. The neighborhood is full of incredible murals and local art connected to the Chicano Mural Movement, and it tells an important story about the culture and community that helped shape Denver. 
SIMMS: Downtown Denver has experienced significant change since the pandemic (and) it’s important to celebrate how far we’ve come, from reopening 16th street, to reactivating our beloved downtown public spaces and bringing our unhoused neighbors indoors. I would, and have, taken my out of town friends to the heart of Downtown Denver to see a show, enjoy a drink or a meal on 16th street, or to see a show at one of our amazing venues. Soon to be home to every Denver sports team, House District 5 has so much to offer!
What do residents in your district say are the community’s biggest issues, and how will you work to address it?
SANDOVAL: One of the biggest issues I hear from residents is a little more abstract than the usual policy conversations about housing, affordability, or public safety. People feel increasingly disconnected from each other and from the neighborhoods they call home. Our district includes the heart of Denver and some of the city’s most historic communities, and people want to make sure that as Denver grows, we don’t lose the sense of community that makes these neighborhoods special. As a state House candidate, I want to help unite our district by investing in the things that bring people together. That means improving public transit and accessibility so our neighborhoods are better connected and easier for everyone to navigate. It means supporting small businesses, especially local restaurants and neighborhood storefronts that serve as gathering places but are struggling with rising costs and rent.  This district needs more diverse and attainable housing options so longtime residents, young families, workers, artists, and newcomers alike can afford to live and build community here. Denver should continue to grow, but in a way that keeps our neighborhoods welcoming, connected, and accessible to people from all backgrounds. 
SIMMS: When talking to my neighbors in House District 5, the challenges they raise are often the same. Many are struggling to keep up with the rising costs of housing, many are heartbroken by the scenes of addiction and mental illness that is plaguing so many in our community, they’re worried about the safety of their streets, and the quality of the air they breathe and the water they drink. These are all symptoms of our deeply entrenched crisis of inequality. I want to address these crises by addressing the root causes, not simply the symptoms. I want to leverage a public bank to provide the cheapest access to capital for housing development across the entire housing spectrum, bringing units online to reduce the costs of housing across the board. I want to invest in services across the entire spectrum of recovery. You need to meet our most vulnerable residents where they are, and when the services they rely on don’t exist, they have no choice but to get left behind. And finally, I want to divest our tax dollars from extractive industry which continues to pollute our communities in pursuit of private profits.
This was the second year in a row the Legislature had to make deep program cuts to balance the state budget. Where can the state reduce its spending, and what is your view on how Colorado can return to a positive budget situation?
SANDOVAL: Colorado’s budget situation is honestly exhausting to watch because every year we end up having the same conversation about cutting services people depend on the most. Our schools are comically underfunded, healthcare costs are through the roof, and communities need more support, but TABOR keeps the state stuck with one hand tied behind its back. I don’t think the answer is cutting programs that help working families, kids, seniors, people with disabilities, or people struggling to get by. I support getting rid of TABOR and updating Colorado’s outdated tax code, including moving toward a graduated income tax so the wealthiest people pay more instead of putting all the financial pressure on everyday Coloradans. I support legislation that would help Colorado actually invest in public education, healthcare, disability services, housing, and transportation instead of constantly fighting over scraps. Colorado is a wealthy state. We should be able to fund good schools, accessible communities, functioning transit, and basic services without acting like that’s unrealistic. People are tired of hearing there’s never enough money while costs keep rising and communities keep being asked to settle for less.
SIMMS: We have to be clear-eyed about the fact that further cuts in state spending will continue to diminish the quality of human services that our neighbors rely on every day. The solution to our budget crisis requires more than cutting spending, and raising revenue continues to be a challenge under TABOR. We need to become the second state in the nation to charter a public bank off of North Dakota’s model to maximize the impact of the tax revenue we already collect. Simply by diverting our tax dollars out of Wall Street, institutions will provide the revenue stream we need not only to fix our structural deficit, but to generate excess revenue which can be returned to the state’s general fund in the form of a dividend.
What policies should the state enact regarding the proliferation of data centers?
SANDOVAL: Data centers, especially in Denver, have become one of the biggest topics of concern across the nation right now because people feel like these projects are being forced into neighborhoods with zero transparency, zero regard for the long-term impact on the community, and almost no real public input. I believe the state should enact much stronger policies around where data centers can be built, how much water and energy they are allowed to use, and whether communities actually want them there in the first place. That includes stricter environmental review standards, limits on water consumption, protections against building these facilities near residential neighborhoods, and giving local communities real power to reject projects that do not align with their needs. Colorado is already dealing with water scarcity, rising energy demands, and the realities of climate change. Water should be for people, agriculture, and life first, not machines. I am not against technology or economic growth, but I do not think corporations should be able to come into our communities, drain resources, and reshape neighborhoods without accountability.
SIMMS: We need to understand that data centers will be needed for our own domestic use of AI. The concerns held by community are very real. They’re scared about their water being contaminated, their energy costs rising and environmentally sensitive spaces being contaminated further. I think we need to pass legislation as a state that ensures our data centers aren’t adding onto the negative impacts communities already face from industry. We need to ensure that our data centers conform to the highest standards of environmental responsibility, and we must protect rate payers from increases in energy and water use rate hikes.
What is your view on working across the aisle, and within your own party, to advance policy?

We all know how cold Colorado winters can get, so I would also defend funding for Low-income Energy Assistance Programs (LEAP) which helps families pay a portion of their winter home heating costs. All other programs in the state budget must be seriously scrutinized line-by-line and evaluated based on whether data shows they are effective uses of taxpayer dollars.

What policies should the state enact regarding the proliferation of data centers? 
GARCIA IRLANDO: I support strict regulations on data centers to protect communities, our water and our climate. For decades the oil and gas industry has polluted our communities and natural resources while the state Legislature and utilities have provided incentives and regulatory exemptions to this industry. I strongly oppose the same playbook proposed by data centers that would bind our state in deficit contracts, leave accountability to the will of corporations, and bypass any safeguards against polluting our communities. I support data center accountability policies such as public health and cumulative impact safeguards, strict water use and conservation parameters, renewable energy requirements, and mandates to ensure any new public utility infrastructure built to provide service to data centers is fully paid for by data center developers and not taxpayers or utility ratepayers. I also support enacting these policies with enforceable oversight mechanisms to ensure data center corporations do not treat noncompliance as the cost of doing business. Given these proposed parameters and accountability measures, I support a moratorium on data centers to guarantee protections for communities, public health, and our water and climate.
CARRERA: Data centers use about as much water as a small town. And considering the rest of Denver can’t even water its lawn right now, it’s not the right time to allow a gargantuan building to guzzle what little water we have. Estimates also show that data centers are expected to account for 12% of all U.S. energy consumption by 2028. Unless they’re able to run on renewable energy and not increase energy costs for residents, I’m a “no” on allowing them to come into our communities.
What is your view on working across the aisle, and within your own party, to advance policy? 
GARCIA IRLANDO: I will work with anyone who wants to work to improve the lives of working people, protect the environment, create universal healthcare and childcare, and make Colorado more affordable for all of us, regardless of party. I will not compromise my values, regardless of party. As someone who has spent my career as a community organizer, nonprofit leader, and working collaboratively in coalitions across Colorado and nationally, I strongly believe that policy should not be decided in silos, but rather built in direct partnership with the people who are most impacted by those decisions. I was recently endorsed by Senator Bernie Sanders, an unaffiliated elected official, who understands that injustice is not a partisan issue, thus the solutions must also be grounded in the impacts to real people and not partisanship. I am excited to carry this approach to the Colorado Legislature, to work collaboratively but also fight when needed, to get things done.
CARRERA: Whenever I helped veterans connect with Social Security benefits, I never asked for their party affiliation. Whenever I connected people experiencing homelessness with housing, I never asked who they voted for in the last presidential election. None of that matters. What matters is helping people, and I’ll link arms with anyone who is interested in putting forward solutions to help the 6 million people who call Colorado home, regardless of whether they’re Democrats or Republicans. Ideas can only get sharper by having conversations with people we disagree with – people who have vastly different life experiences from my own. And that’s what I plan to do as state senator.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Attorney General threatens legal action against six abortion pill providers
description: The Alabama Attorney General’s Office on Tuesday threatened legal action against six companies that it said were advertising or distributing abortion-inducing medication to Alabamians. “Alabama’s law is clear, abortion is illegal in this state. These companies are not only breaking the law, they are deceiving Alabama consumers about the very real dangers of[...]
text:
Mifepristone is one of two drugs that can be used before 10 weeks to terminate a pregnancy and to treat miscarriages. The Alabama Attorney General's Office on Tuesday threatened legal action against six companies that distribute the medication to consumers in the state that has a near-total abortion ban. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images) 


Key points

The Alabama Attorney General’s Office on Tuesday threatened legal action against six companies it said were advertising or distributing medication to induce abortions, citing Alabama law that makes performing or attempting to perform an abortion a felony.
The office cited a study from a conservative think tank on abortion pill complications that has drawn criticism over its methodology.
A reproductive rights advocate said the letter was “an enormous commercial” for the companies.
The letters were signed by Deputy Attorney General Katherine Robertson, who is competing in next week’s Republican runoff for attorney general and who has been criticized by her opponent, former Alabama Supreme Court Justice Jay Mitchell, for accepting contributions from a man who has criticized Alabama’s near-total abortion ban.




The Alabama Attorney General’s Office on Tuesday threatened legal action against six companies that it said were advertising or distributing abortion-inducing medication to Alabamians.
“Alabama’s law is clear, abortion is illegal in this state. These companies are not only breaking the law, they are deceiving Alabama consumers about the very real dangers of these drugs. That stops now,” Attorney General Steve Marshall said in a statement. “Anyone who tries to exploit Alabamians for profit while flouting our laws will be prosecuted to the fullest extent permitted by law.”
In doing so, the office effectively advertised where Alabamians seeking an abortion can get medication, said Robin Marty, executive director of the West Alabama Women’s Center, which provided abortion care before Roe v. Wade was overturned in 2022.
“As a person who is heavily involved in reproductive access for all people, I am surprised that he does not realize that what he has done has essentially provided an enormous commercial for these companies,” Marty said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Alabama’s near-total ban on abortion, passed in 2019, went into effect in 2022 after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down federal abortion protections in the Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization ruling, with exceptions for when the mother’s life is in danger. A performed or attempted abortion is a Class C felony under the ban, punishable by up to 10 years in prison, but the person seeking the abortion is not civilly or criminally liable.
Marty said the Attorney General’s Office’s press release told Alabamians where they could get medication for an abortion, which is something she cannot do as a provider.
“That has now improved the ability for people to find out where they can access abortion in a way that we were never able to actually let people know before, which is ironic, since we had been told that telling people where these companies were was in fact a criminal conspiracy,” she said.
The cease-and-desist letters were sent to Plan C, Southern Woven, ybycmeds, Abortion Pills in Private, Red State Access and Cambridge Reproductive Health Consultants. The letters demand the companies stop all advertising, sale and delivery of abortion-inducing drugs to Alabama consumers. Failure to do so, according to the statement, will result in an investigation and potential legal action.
Messages seeking comment from the companies were sent Tuesday afternoon.
According to the Federal Drug and Food Administration (FDA), the combination of drugs is safe to use up to 70 days of gestation. A 2015 study published by Dr. Michael Creinin, an OB-GYN at the University of California Davis Health who has researched the safety of mifepristone since studies first began in 1992, found that severe outcomes from mifepristone use requiring blood transfusion and hospitalization occurred in less than 1% of cases. 
Rhetoric versus reality: Facts about the abortion pill

The letters from the Attorney General’s Office cite a 2025 analysis by the Ethics and Public Policy Center, a D.C.-based think tank that applies “the riches of the Jewish and Christian traditions to contemporary questions of law, culture, and politics,” found that 10.9% of women that took the medication experienced sepsis, infection or hemorrhaging within 45 days of taking it. The center partners with the Alliance Defending Freedom, a conservative organization that brought the Dobbs case. 
Experts dispute that the center defines a serious adverse event the same way the FDA does, as a condition requiring hospitalization; threatens the life of a patient or causes disability and permanent damage or death. Creinin also criticized the methodology used by the center, saying in some cases it double-counted issues experienced by one patient.
The letters are signed by Deputy Attorney General Katherine Robertson, who is in the Republican runoff for Attorney General. Through the campaign, Robertson’s opponent Jay Mitchell, a former Alabama Supreme Court Justice, has criticized Robertson for accepting a $150,000 donation from Hugh Culverhouse Jr., a philanthropist who donated $250,000 to Planned Parenthood Southeast in 2019.
Messages seeking comment from the Robertson and Mitchell campaigns were left Wednesday afternoon.
According to reporting from Alabama Daily News, the University of Alabama’s law school was once named for Culverhouse but the school parted ways after Culverhouse was critical of the state’s abortion ban. In a 2019 Wall Street Journal ad, Culverhouse called for a boycott of the state because of the “unconstitutional and barbaric law.”
The Attorney General’s Office on Wednesday joined 13 other states in a letter to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) calling for tighter controls on mifepristone. Marshall said in a statement that as medical waste from the medication is discarded, it contaminates drinking water.
“There is a booming black-market for drug-inducing abortions operating completely outside of lawful medical oversight, and it has created a serious public health crisis. This is not just for those obtaining and using these illegal and dangerous drugs,” Marshall said.
Multiple states have considered legislation to create environmental restrictions around the drug or bills requiring providers to instruct patients to collect fetal tissue in medical waste kits and return it to the provider rather than flush it. The EPA may also conduct a review that could be used to restrict access in the future.
In 1996, the FDA Center for Drug Evaluation and Research issued a finding of no significant impact on the water supply from mifepristone.
Marty said that while the press release helped patients in a way that providers legally cannot, the state is focused on the wrong things when it comes to women’s health.
Alabama infant mortality rate improves, but remains higher than national average

“They’re not doing anything to improve health care access for the people who are not getting abortions. There have been no moves to improve maternal health care in this state. There has been no moves to improve access or provide more support for contraception in this state,” she said. “At this point it seems that they are far more interested in making sure that nobody is able to access a safe abortion than they are making sure that our hospitals are not letting Black women die in childbirth.”
According to state data for 2020-2021, the maternal mortality rate for white mothers was 28.2 deaths per 100,000 live births. The maternal mortality rate for Black mothers was 77 deaths per 100,000 live births.
Only 30% of Alabama’s rural hospitals have labor and delivery units, leaving many expectant parents to drive long distances for care. Providence Hospital in Mobile announced on May 14 that it is closing its labor and delivery unit this summer. 
Key points box was written by Editor Brian Lyman.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: You are witnessing an independent movement in Idaho politics
description: Something is happening in Idaho politics this year that I have not seen in the 50 years I have followed politics in our great state: The emergence of credible and well-financed independent candidates running for major political office. It is as if we are seeing the emergence of a new political movement developing right in […]
text:
A "vote here" sign welcomes voters for the May 19, 2026, primary election at Westside Elementary School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Something is happening in Idaho politics this year that I have not seen in the 50 years I have followed politics in our great state: The emergence of credible and well-financed independent candidates running for major political office.
It is as if we are seeing the emergence of a new political movement developing right in front of our eyes. 
For years I have believed that the future of good, reasonable, moderate to right of center politics in Idaho is what I call fusion politics. Fusion politics is where Republicans, Democrats and independents who are unhappy with their party’s candidates join hands to take back their state and nation.
They can build a better future for our state and our nation without losing their identity as a Republican, Democrat or independent. But they vote for the best person out of loyalty to their fellow citizens, democracy and the Constitution. 
We have seen for many years now where the traditional Republican and Democratic Party primaries are not working. Especially in the Idaho GOP primary, they give us general election candidates who cannot work across the aisle, compromise and find solutions that address kitchen-table issues that impact people’s lives.
In other cases, primaries produce challengers with little or no chance of winning the general election. As a result, our state and national politics remain polarized, gridlocked and ineffective.
We just saw this play out in Idaho’s panhandle where Republican central committees, which have become radicalized, united to defeat effective and thoughtful lawmakers like Jim Woodward, Mark Sauter and Lori McCann. 
On the national stage, we saw the same thing happening with President Donald Trump taking out his revenge on Republicans who did not kiss his ring 100 percent of the time. For example, Texas Sen. John Cornyn was recently defeated by Trump-endorsed Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is one of the most corrupt politicians in Texas history. His fellow Republican lawmakers even impeached him. 
The Democrats now have the best chance in more than 30 years of electing their candidate, James Talarico. We are also seeing independent candidates emerging in Montana and Nebraska with the support of the Democratic establishment. Why? Because they have the best chance of beating far-right GOP candidates.
Because primary elections often nominate candidates who are either too extreme or unlikely to win, many voters are looking for a better option. That’s what we are seeing now in Idaho. 
Todd Achilles, a former Democratic state lawmaker, is running as an independent against 83-year-old Jim Risch, who has spent his entire adult life in political office. Achilles is a veteran and business entrepreneur who has a real chance to defeat the incumbent senator who has lost touch with both his constituents and the U.S. Constitution.
As chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Risch is the third most powerful person when it comes to our international relations. And yet he has decided not to lead when the world is on fire with the first European war since World War II and Trump’s new war with Iran which is costing the country lives and treasure and causing prices to skyrocket for families. 
In the governor’s race, former Idaho Supreme Court Justice John Stegner is running as an independent against two-term Gov. Brad Little, who may be the most vulnerable incumbent since Don Samuelson in 1970. Stegner is a right-of-center candidate in the style of Republican Governor Phil Batt and Senator Jim McClure. 
Stegner is tapping into those Republicans who are disillusioned with Brad Little’s leadership, independents, and even Democrats who believe he has a good chance of knocking off Little in the general election. 
In the 1st Congressional District, Sarah Zabel is running as an independent against 1st District Congressman Russ Fulcher who has even supported the transfer of public lands to the states, a politically perilous stance. But Fulcher believes he is invincible because he has won re-election easily in the past. 
But Zabel has come along and stands a good chance of giving Fulcher his toughest run yet. Zabel is not a lightweight. She is a retired Air Force General who served her country for 31 years. She is a former Republican who became an independent because the Republican Party made it “clear it no longer stands for the principles I believe in: free markets, fiscal responsibility, limited government, a strong defense, and the rule of law.” 
So, what’s not to like about these three independent candidates for Idaho? Nothing. They are the full package – thoughtful, bipartisan, collaborative, with significant life experiences that would make them valuable public servants.
The only problem is that they also face Democratic challengers in addition to the Republican incumbents they want to unseat. With two candidates challenging the incumbents, the vote will split, and the incumbents will waltz to re-election. Then we will continue to have the cycle of dysfunction, extremism and polarization. 
Some people argue that the Democrats who emerged from the May primary do not have a chance to win. None of them have an electoral history that shows they can win 50 percent of the vote, plus one. Yet the party has supported them knowing their past records. 
There is an example from Idaho political history that is instructive here.
In 1966, an ultra-conservative state senator from Sandpoint named Don Samuelson defeated incumbent Republican Gov. Robert Smylie in the primary. That prompted a more moderate Republican senator named Perry Swisher to run as independent candidate.
In the Democratic primary, a Salmon lawyer named Charles Herndon defeated a state senator named Cecil Andrus by about 1,300 votes and a third candidate, William J. Dee, by a larger margin. Andrus thought his political career was over. But Herndon was killed in a plane crash while campaigning seven weeks before the November election. 
A battle ensued in the Democratic State Central Committee to see who would replace Herndon on the ticket. The natural choice would have been Andrus since he finished a close second behind Herndon. But Democratic boss, Tom Boise, supported a more conservative candidate, Max Hanson, Federal Agricultural Services director for Idaho.
It was a bitter contest which Hanson was confident he would win thanks to the backing of party boss Boise. What Hanson and Boise did not consider was that Idaho’s two-term Democratic U.S. Sen. Frank Church quietly supported Andrus behind the scenes. Church believed that Andrus would be the strongest candidate against Samuelson. 
Church had his politically savvy chief of staff Verda Barnes help round up central committee votes for Andrus. With support from Church and Barnes, Andrus eked out a victory by two votes. 
In November, Swisher and Andrus split the vote, and Samuelson won re-election by a narrow margin over Andrus. If Swisher, the less electable candidate, had gotten out of the race Andrus stood a good chance of becoming the first Democratic governor in 25 years.
But the central committee’s decision to back Andrus, the strongest candidate, set the party up for success in the decades to come.
Four years later Andrus beat Samuelson and went on to get elected governor three more times, twice in landslides. He did it by attracting a coalition of Republican, Democrat, and independent voters – a fusion of voters.
Thanks to his popularity with voters of all stripes, Andrus changed the course of Idaho history, giving Democrats control of the governor’s office for the next 24 years. That control was broken when Andrus’ friend, Republican Phil Batt was elected governor, and he strengthened the party which gave the GOP control of the governor’s office for the last 32 years.
There are two things we can learn from the 1966 election.
First, politics is about winning, not running for office. To win an election, you must have the strongest candidate in the race. That candidate can be a Democrat or Republican turned independent as we have seen in the case of Achilles, Stegner and Zabel.
But it must be candidate who can attract Republicans, Democrats and independents and create a “fusion movement.”  
If Frank Church and the Democratic Central Committee did not have the wisdom to replace Herndon with Andrus, clearly the strongest candidate, the trajectory of Idaho politics would have turned out much different. And a once-in-a-generation leader would not have had a chance to serve his state and nation.
The second lesson from 1966 is that the weakest of the two challengers must drop out so that the strongest candidate can have a clear pathway to victory. Otherwise, they will split the vote, and the incumbent will sleepwalk toward reelection.
It takes a strong ego to run for political office, and there is nothing wrong with that. But to serve the best interest of one’s fellow citizens sometimes it is necessary to set one’s ego aside, drop out of a race, and back the strongest candidate who can win. 
Rod Gramer is an Idaho native, longtime journalist and advocate for public education. He is also co-author of “Fighting the Odds, the Life of Senator Frank Church,” and “Lucky, The Wit and Wisdom of Governor Phil Batt.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Bridge Program sees success encouraging WV kids in foster, kinship care to graduate from high school
description: Going into her junior year of high school, Raynbow Carter/Freeman described herself as “lost.” In 2023, the teenager’s mother died, then she moved in with a family member in Kanawha County. “I didn’t have anybody at the time,” she said. Then, her junior year of high school, things changed. She received a mentor at Nitro […]
text:
Raynbow Carter/Freeman (left), who recently graduated from Nitro High School, stands with her Bridge Program mentor, Kelly Price. (Courtesy photo)Going into her junior year of high school, Raynbow Carter/Freeman described herself as “lost.” In 2023, the teenager’s mother died, then she moved in with a family member in Kanawha County.
“I didn’t have anybody at the time,” she said.
Then, her junior year of high school, things changed. She received a mentor at Nitro High School through the Bridge Program, a nonprofit support service for children in foster or kinship care. 
Carter/Freeman said her mentor, Kelly Price, helped her do everything, like finish classes to graduate and fill out applications for college financial aid. Price offered to buy her a prom dress and yearbook. 
“Honestly, she was the mother that I needed when I didn’t actually have,” said Carter/Freeman, 18, who recently graduated from Nitro High School.
This year, 98% of seniors — 125 individuals — in Mission West Virginia’s Bridge Program graduated with a high school diploma and concrete future plans, according to program leaders.
The program just wrapped up its ninth school year of academic mentorship, serving nearly 600 high school students in West Virginia’s overwhelmed foster care system and those living in kinship care without state involvement. 
“The one thing that our kids all have in common is just they need support, they need stability. They need a person that’s there,” said Darlinda McCumbers, a Bridge Program mentor at Clay County High School. “These kids have been, from my experience, been let down a lot by adults. Through this program here, they have someone that is stable in their school that is making an effort, making sure they’re there encouraging them.”
Youth in foster care and kinship care regularly face barriers to finishing high school, including school instability, multiple moves through the foster care system, poverty, trauma and limited support systems.
Students are referred to the Bridge Program by teachers, school counselors, staff and, sometimes, their older siblings who have already participated. 
Program mentors in high schools focus on improving attendance, grades, school participation and working toward graduation. 
“The mentors have access to their online school platforms, and they can start seeing which assignments are missing,” said Kelly Thompson, executive director of Mission West Virginia. “They take these overwhelming problems that look like a problem to the child, where they’re going to give up hope, and they’re working on those tasks one by one.”
The goal for each child in the Bridge Program is to graduate on time with a plan in place for after graduation. Many times the children don’t realize higher education is an option, mentors said.
“We work with them from freshman until senior (year) … We focus on finding resources and funding to help get them to where they need to be. We’re a big advocate,” McCumbers said. 
“They realize they do have what it takes to succeed, they do have what it takes to go to college, go to a trade school, or apply for that job they didn’t think that they could be qualified to do,” she added. 
Bridge Program Manager Ashley Arthur said they’re able to provide transportation so students can visit college campuses. 
“Transportation is a huge barrier, especially for our kids in these rural areas, like Clay County,” she said. “Our mentors, and at Mission (West Virginia), we have funded field trip opportunities, both big and small, so kids can actually go. A lot of them are setting foot on a college campus for the first time, and they’re able to see themselves there.”
Raynbow Carter/Freeman (Courtesy photo)
Carter/Freeman didn’t think she would be able to go to college before she entered the Bridge Program. She will attend Marshall University in the fall to study social work and participate in the Marching Thunder Color Guard.
“I really want to help people. I want to be the mental help that Kelly was for me, because when I didn’t have somebody to talk to, I knew that I had Kelly to talk to,” Carter/Freeman said. 
Price, a Bridge Program mentor at Nitro High School, said she was very proud of Carter/Freeman.
“(In) our first conversation, she didn’t want to go to college, but now you can see where she is,” Price said. “My door was always open to her if she ever needed to come in.”
Program would like to expand beyond seven counties 
The highest percentage of West Virginia’s roughly 5,900 foster children are in kinship care, meaning they live with a family member. In some counties, 50% of grandparents are raising their grandchildren, often due to the state’s drug epidemic. 
“We also work with the grandparents in that process too, because sometimes, especially if they’re kinship, they worry a lot about money for college,” McCumbers said.
The Bridge Program has been implemented through Check and Connect, a nationally recognized dropout prevention model. 
The program was originally piloted in Clay County before expanding to Boone, Cabell, Kanawha, Lincoln, Putnam and Wood counties. 
This year, more than a dozen students who moved to a different county mid-school year due to foster care or housing disruptions were able to seamlessly transition into another Bridge Program at a new school.
The program is largely funded by foundation funding. It has also received money from the West Virginia First Foundation, which is managing the state’s opioid settlement dollars.
Thompson said she they’re working toward expanding the program into more counties.
“It’s about $2,000 per student each school year, so it’s fairly low cost to have a mentor placed in a school and to work with that population,” she said. “So, it would just look like securing more stable funding.”
The program currently operates on a $1 million budget to serve 600 kids with full-time mentoring services. 
Mission West Virginia is a statewide nonprofit organization focused on supporting vulnerable youth, including foster children. Their work includes recruiting foster families providing life skills education to youth.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Three Johns and a Will for justice: When Tennessee’s white leaders spoke out
description: Last week Tennessee Lookout Editor Holly McCall published a piece titled: The Silence of Tennessee’s ‘statesmen’ drawing our attention to previous governors and leaders (across political parties) who have remained silent before and after the last-minute redistricting aimed specifically at obliterating Black votes in Memphis. It’s right to honor the many Tenn[...]
text:
The late Rev. Bernard LaFayette visits the farm of Rev. Will Campbell on Nov. 18, 2022. Campbell, a Baptist minister nicknamed the "Bootleg Preacher," was a Southern white man active in the Civil Rights Movement. He died in 2013. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Last week Tennessee Lookout Editor Holly McCall published a piece titled: The Silence of Tennessee’s ‘statesmen’ drawing our attention to previous governors and leaders (across political parties) who have remained silent before and after the last-minute redistricting aimed specifically at obliterating Black votes in Memphis. 
It’s right to honor the many Tennessee Black leaders who have stood up for civil rights, often putting their bodies in harm’s way and livelihoods at risk, but white leaders today should be speaking out, too, to take a stand against injustice, and there is some historic precedent here in the state.
The eerie silence of former Tennessee leaders has been disturbing for many of us. In her editorial, McCall ponders how Howard Baker, a long-time Republican U.S. Senator who was known for brokering bipartisan deals and encouraging civil discourse might respond to what is occurring in Tennessee. 
 These days, ‘civil discourse’ feels like something that might be encased behind glass at a museum memorializing the before times when the water filtration system at our state Capital hadn’t yet started pumping MAGA infused water into the fountains.   
Editor’s notebook: The silence of Tennessee’s ‘statesmen’ 

For those of us with three decades or more of Nashville residency under our exhausted belts, it has been disturbing to witness former leaders stand idly by while hard-fought for civil rights have been dealt a lethal blow. 
 And McCall’s piece got me thinking how not long ago we lived among ‘city fathers’ who used their privilege and influence to challenge bigotry and racism and tweak the consciences of the powerful. It wasn’t always so uncommon for white leaders to speak out on controversial issues of race. 
 Who were these ‘city fathers’ who served as mentors to hundreds (maybe thousands) fortunate enough to inhabit their sphere? Probably many of us experienced these men up close as they found time to have coffee or lunch and share stories that prepared the next generation to carry on work they (unfortunately) knew would be necessary. 
Probably most well-known is John Seigenthaler who in 1961, as a young U.S. Justice Department aide was brutally attacked with a pipe by Ku Klux Klansmen as he rushed to protect Freedom Riders arriving in Montgomery, Alabama. The Klansmen left Seigenthaler in the street to die but he survived the assault and then spent four decades with the Tennessean as a journalist, eventually becoming editor, publisher and CEO. During his reign, Seigenthaler guided the steadfast coverage of the civil rights movement and exposed the activities of the Ku Klux Klan. Tennessean archives are full of civil rights history in large part because of Seigenthaler.   
 Another John was the colorful and controversial attorney, entrepreneur and former gubernatorial candidate John Jay Hooker, affectionately nicknamed The Duke of Belle Meade and Little Lord Fauntleroy who dedicated the last years of his life to getting money out of politics and promoting civil rights advocacy. Anyone who ever lunched with Hooker heard about the time his private plane was chartered to pick up Muhammad Ali, with whom he shared a deep, decades-long friendship that began in the 1970s and lasted until their deaths. It was this friendship that greatly influenced him and strengthened his commitment to equality. He died in January 2016, before the November election of President Donald Trump.  
 Probably, the quietest of the Johns in demeanor but unparalleled in fierceness is writer and historian John Egerton who packed a wallop with his pen. Egerton spent much of his career writing and agitating against the ways racism and white supremacy mapped the South’s trajectory.  It would be impossible to tally the number of Nashville writers inspired by his words or total those who had the good fortune of having his red pen scribbled all over a rough draft. In November 2013 John Egerton quietly slipped out of life as if late for his next appointment.  
 And then there was inimitable Southern Baptist preacher and author, Rev. Will D. Campbell, who in 1957 walked nine Black school children through hostile crowds to integrate public schools in Little Rock, Arkansas. The only white person present at the founding of Martin Luther King, Jr.’s Southern Christian Leadership Conference, SCLC, Campbell was committed to the sacredness of all life.  
Always controversial, Campbell began meeting and ministering to the enemies of integration, the Klu Klux Klan, believing that like those on death row, everyone deserved mercy. Having spent the last years of his life in a log cabin in Mt. Juliet, the man affectionately known as ‘the bootleg preacher’ sadly died in 2013.
 While these four white men knew and respected one another, they inhabited separate worlds but shared something in common: a commitment to justice. They all courageously used whatever privilege and influence they possessed by standing side-by-side and in proximity to Black and brown brothers and sisters, and anyone disenfranchised. They spoke truth to power and didn’t shrink from confrontation.  
 And while former Govs. Phil Bredesen and Bill Haslam purport to tackle political “differences” on a podcast named “You Might Be Right,” they’ve virtually remained silent as state legislators hacked up voting districts like a pig at a barbecue — in broad daylight.  And that is hard to digest. The podcast title and the content functions less as a bipartisan meeting of the minds, and more as a siren call for complacency, tempting Tennesseans towards agreeing with, or at least being apathetic to, what the right is doing to our state and country. 
 Let me be clear. The two former governors are not the only powerful men of political privilege standing quietly in the shadows. And it’s not just ‘men of power’.  There are a handful of extremely powerful Southern men and women who seem to have misplaced their tongues in the face of overt fascism. That these individuals have chosen silence these past several years as the Trump-obsessed legislature fomented fear and loathing while passing bills that target immigrants, trans people, women and anyone dark skinned is deeply troubling — some might even say, appalling.  
 As far as the triumvirate of Johns and a Will for justice, having known and been mentored by each of them, it is highly doubtful that any of them is giving a heavenly thumbs up for a light-hearted podcast called ‘You might be Right’ in the face of so much wrong.
